Introduction and meaning
Keeping lottery office. BNS restatement of IPC 294A. Elements are substantially the same; cite the BNS number for offences on or after 1 July 2024. BNS restatement of IPC 294A. Cite the BNS number for facts on or after 1 July 2024.
In student language: BNS s. 297 is the rule on “Keeping lottery office”. The section provides that (1) Whoever keeps any office or place for the purpose of drawing any lottery not being a State lottery or a lottery authorised by the State Government, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to six months, or with fine, or with both. Do not stop at the heading. An examiner awards marks for the ingredients, the explanations and the illustrations, not for writing the title alone.

Why this is asked
Criminal law arguments turn on statutory ingredients. BNS s. 297 exists so that “Keeping lottery office” has a closed legal test in Chapter XV — Of Offences Affecting the Public Health, Safety, Convenience, Decency and Morals. An authoritative analysis defines the concept, lists every ingredient, walks the statutory illustrations, states exceptions, and applies the test methodically to facts.
Chapter setting: Nuisance, adulteration, rash driving, obscenity, lottery.

The provision in detail
297. (1) Whoever keeps any office or place for the purpose of drawing any lottery not being a State lottery or a lottery authorised by the State Government, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to six months, or with fine, or with both

(2) Whoever publishes any proposal to pay any sum, or to deliver any goods, or to do or forbear from doing anything for the benefit of any person, on any event or contingency relative or applicable to the drawing of any ticket, lot, number or figure in any such lottery, shall be punished with fine which may extend to five thousand rupees

hypotheticals.analysis:
Step 1 — Identify the provision. The correct current-law cite is BNS s. 297 (Keeping lottery office), Chapter XV — Of Offences Affecting the Public Health, Safety, Convenience, Decency and Morals.
Step 2 — State the legal test in your own words, then list the ingredients:
   (1) Whoever keeps any office or place for the purpose of drawing any lottery not being a State lottery or a lottery authorised by the State Government, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to six months, or with fine, or with both
   (2) Whoever publishes any proposal to pay any sum, or to deliver any goods, or to do or forbear from doing anything for the benefit of any person, on any event or contingency relative or applicable to the drawing of any ticket, lot, number or figure in any such lottery, shall be punished with fine which may extend to five thousand rupees
Step 3 — Check limitations, provisos and the rest of the Chapter so you do not apply s. 297 in a vacuum.
Step 4 — Map each fact to an ingredient. Write “this fact proves ingredient (a)” or “this fact is missing, so the section is not made out”.
Step 5 — Conclude. If every essential ingredient is proved and no exception covers the case, BNS s. 297 applies. If any essential ingredient fails, say so and stop. Do not invent a different section to save the answer.

enhancement.detailedExplanation: Section 297 constitutes a key component of Chapter XV (Of Offences Affecting the Public Health, Safety, Convenience, Decency and Morals) of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, addressing keeping lottery office. The provision balances personal liberty with public interest and social order. The prosecution must establish every statutory element beyond reasonable doubt: the specified actus reus, the requisite mens rea, and any relevant statutory circumstances. Modern judicial interpretation emphasizes substantive fairness, proportionality in sentencing, and adherence to constitutional safeguards. Where statutory exceptions or provisos are attached to the section, the accused must establish facts bringing the case within such provisions under evidentiary standards.
examples: Teaching example (Standard application): An individual intentionally commits acts satisfying the statutory formula of keeping lottery office under Section 297 without lawful authority. The individual is liable under BNS s. 297.

Teaching example (Absence of mens rea / Lawful exception): A person acts in good faith or without the requisite statutory mental element under circumstances recognized by law. The essential ingredients of Section 297 are not satisfied; no penal liability attaches.
distinctions: Section 297 vs General Attempt: Section 297 penalizes the substantive conduct specified in Chapter XV; inchoate attempts without specific provisions fall under the general attempt provisions.

Section 297 vs Cognate Chapter Offences: Liability under Section 297 is distinguished by its specific mental threshold and the particular legal interest protected under Of Offences Affecting the Public Health, Safety, Convenience, Decency and Morals.
problemApplication: Issue: Whether the accused is liable under BNS s. 297 for conduct relating to keeping lottery office.
Rule: Under BNS s. 297, liability attaches upon proof of the statutory actus reus accompanied by the requisite mens rea without lawful justification.
Application: The evidence demonstrates that the accused performed the specified act with the required state of mind, satisfying all statutory ingredients of Section 297.
Conclusion: The accused is guilty of an offence under BNS s. 297 and subject to the prescribed punishment.
